title: Count Beautiful Splits in an Array
statement:
Split `nums` at two places into three non-empty contiguous parts `nums1`, `nums2` and `nums3`, which in this order make up the whole array. A split is beautiful when `nums1` is a prefix of `nums2`, or `nums2` is a prefix of `nums3` (one condition is enough; both may hold).

An array `a` is a prefix of an array `b` when `b` begins with all of `a`'s elements in the same order, so `a` is never longer than `b` and may equal it.

Return the number of beautiful splits; two splits are different when they cut at different positions. An array with fewer than 3 elements cannot be split this way, so its answer is 0.
notes:
## Intuition

A split is fixed by two cut points: `nums2` starts at index `i` and `nums3` at index `j`, with `1 <= i < j < n`. Trying every pair and comparing the parts element by element costs O(n³). Both tests really ask one question, how far two suffixes of `nums` agree, so answer it once for every pair of suffixes: `lcp[i][j]` is the length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes starting at `i` and at `j`. As in LCS-style two-sequence DP, a match at `(i, j)` extends the match at `(i + 1, j + 1)` by one, so the table fills in O(n²) and each test becomes O(1).

## Approach

1. Make `lcp` an `(n + 1) x (n + 1)` table of zeros; the extra row and column stand for empty suffixes.
2. Fill it from the bottom row up: when `nums[i] === nums[j]`, set `lcp[i][j] = lcp[i + 1][j + 1] + 1`; otherwise the cell stays 0.
3. For every cut pair `i < j`, the parts have lengths `i`, `j - i` and `n - j`.
4. `nums1` is a prefix of `nums2` when it is not longer (`i <= j - i`) and the suffixes at `0` and `i` agree on at least `i` values (`lcp[0][i] >= i`).
5. `nums2` is a prefix of `nums3` when `j - i <= n - j` and `lcp[i][j] >= j - i`.
6. Add 1 to `count` when either test passes.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 1, 2, 1]`, so `n = 4`. The table gives `lcp[0][1] = 1` (the suffixes `[1, 1, 2, 1]` and `[1, 2, 1]` share one value) and `lcp[2][3] = 0` (`2` against `1`).

- `i = 1, j = 2`: lengths 1, 1, 2; `1 <= 1` and `lcp[0][1] = 1 >= 1`, so it is beautiful.
- `i = 1, j = 3`: lengths 1, 2, 1; `1 <= 2` and `lcp[0][1] >= 1`, so it is beautiful.
- `i = 2, j = 3`: `nums1` (2 values) is longer than `nums2` (1 value), and `lcp[2][3] = 0 < 1`, so it is not.

`count` ends at 2.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): every table cell and every cut pair takes constant work.
- Space: O(n²) for `lcp`.

## Pitfalls

- A long common prefix is not enough by itself: the shorter part must also fit, so check the lengths too.
- Count a split once when both conditions hold; combine them with OR instead of adding two counts.
- Every part is non-empty, so `i` starts at 1 and `j` stops at `n - 1`; arrays of length 1 or 2 give 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `lcp` | `lcp[i][j]`: length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes starting at `i` and `j` |
| `i`, `j` | two suffix starts; while counting, where `nums2` and `nums3` begin |
| `firstIsPrefix` | `nums1` is a prefix of `nums2` |
| `secondIsPrefix` | `nums2` is a prefix of `nums3` |
| `count` | beautiful splits found so far |
